claim: Low-affinity Ultrabithorax (Ubx)-responsive shavenbaby (svb) enhancers drive expression using localized transcriptional environments in Drosophila melanogaster embryos.
source: We previously showed in Drosophila melanogaster embryos that low-affinity Ultrabithorax (Ubx)-responsive shavenbaby (svb) enhancers drive expression using localized transcriptional environments and that active svb enhancers on different chromosomes tended to colocalize (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Active svb enhancers on different chromosomes tend to colocalize.
source: We previously showed in Drosophila melanogaster embryos that low-affinity Ultrabithorax (Ubx)-responsive shavenbaby (svb) enhancers drive expression using localized transcriptional environments and that active svb enhancers on different chromosomes tended to colocalize (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Deleting a redundant enhancer from the svb locus led to reduced trichome numbers in embryos raised at elevated temperatures.
source: Deleting a redundant enhancer from the svb locus led to reduced trichome numbers in embryos raised at elevated temperatures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing trichome counts at different temperatures

claim: The DG3 deletion allele shows lower Ubx concentration at transcription sites.
source: Using high-resolution fluorescence microscopy, we observed lower Ubx concentration and transcriptional output in this deletion allele.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data presented in Figure 3

claim: The DG3 deletion allele shows lower transcriptional output.
source: Using high-resolution fluorescence microscopy, we observed lower Ubx concentration and transcriptional output in this deletion allele.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data presented in Figure 3

claim: Transcription sites of the full svb cis-regulatory region inserted into a different chromosome colocalized with the svb locus.
source: Transcription sites of the full svb cis-regulatory region inserted into a different chromosome colocalized with the svb locus, increasing Ubx concentration, the transcriptional output of svb, and partially rescuing the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4

claim: Colocalization of svbBAC with the svb locus increases Ubx concentration at transcription sites.
source: Transcription sites of the full svb cis-regulatory region inserted into a different chromosome colocalized with the svb locus, increasing Ubx concentration, the transcriptional output of svb, and partially rescuing the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 4F

claim: Colocalization of svbBAC with the svb locus increases the transcriptional output of svb.
source: Transcription sites of the full svb cis-regulatory region inserted into a different chromosome colocalized with the svb locus, increasing Ubx concentration, the transcriptional output of svb, and partially rescuing the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 4E

claim: Colocalization of svbBAC with the svb locus partially rescues the trichome phenotype.
source: Transcription sites of the full svb cis-regulatory region inserted into a different chromosome colocalized with the svb locus, increasing Ubx concentration, the transcriptional output of svb, and partially rescuing the phenotype.
evidence: Supported by trichome counting data in Figure 5D

claim: Multiple enhancers could reinforce a local transcriptional hub to buffer against environmental stresses and genetic perturbations, providing a mechanism for phenotypical robustness.
source: Thus, multiple enhancers could reinforce a local transcriptional hub to buffer against environmental stresses and genetic perturbations, providing a mechanism for phenotypical robustness.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing rescue effects

claim: Transcriptional regulation controls precise patterns of gene-expression during embryogenesis, leading to cell-fate specification.
source: During embryogenesis, transcriptional regulation controls precise patterns of gene-expression, leading to cell-fate specification (Long et al., 2016; Mallo and Alonso, 2013; Reiter et al., 2017; Spitz and Furlong, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature

claim: Transcription factor binding in eukaryotic cell lines and embryos is dynamic but transient, occurring frequently but with each event lasting for at most a few seconds.
source: Live imaging experiments have shown that transcription factor binding in eukaryotic cell lines and embryos is dynamic but transient, occurring frequently but with each event lasting for at most a few seconds (Chen et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Normanno et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to live imaging studies

claim: Many developmental enhancers harbor functionally important low-affinity binding sites.
source: Additionally, recent studies have shown that many developmental enhancers harbor functionally important low-affinity binding sites (Antosova et al., 2016; Crocker et al., 2010; Crocker et al., 2015; Crocker et al., 2016; Farley et al., 2015; Farley et al., 2016; Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Lebrecht et al., 2005; Lorberbaum et al., 2016; Rister et al., 2015; Rowan et al., 2010; Tanay, 2006).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to recent studies

claim: The Homeobox (Hox) family is responsible for body segment identity along the anterior-posterior axis in animals.
source: One example is the Homeobox (Hox) family that is responsible for body segment identity along the anterior-posterior axis in animals.
evidence: Established knowledge in developmental biology

claim: Hox transcription factors descended from a common ancestor and their preferences for binding sequences are very similar.
source: Because Hox transcription factors descended from a common ancestor, their preferences for binding sequences are very similar (Berger et al., 2008; McGinnis and Krumlauf, 1992; Noyes et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to evolutionary and molecular studies

claim: Several enhancers in the shavenbaby (svb) locus make use of low-affinity binding sequences for Ultrabithorax (Ubx) to select for specific Hox factors.
source: To select for specific Hox factors, several enhancers in the shavenbaby (svb) locus make use of low-affinity binding sequences for Ultrabithorax (Ubx) (Crocker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crocker et al., 2015

claim: Svb is a transcription factor that drives the formation of trichomes, epidermal projections on the surface of the segmented fly embryo.
source: Svb is a transcription factor that drives the formation of trichomes, epidermal projections on the surface of the segmented fly embryo (Chanut-Delalande et al., 2006; Delon et al., 2003; Payre et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing svb function

claim: Ubx transiently but repeatedly explores the same physical locations in a nucleus, which are likely clusters of binding sites.
source: We have previously shown in living Drosophila melanogaster embryos that Ubx transiently but repeatedly explores the same physical locations in a nucleus, which are likely clusters of binding sites (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Transcriptional microenvironments of high local Ubx and cofactor concentrations surround active transcription sites driven by low-affinity svb enhancers.
source: We have additionally shown that transcriptional microenvironments of high local Ubx and cofactor concentrations surround active transcription sites driven by low-affinity svb enhancers.
evidence: Refers to previous work by the authors

claim: The distributions of many transcription factors in the nucleus are highly heterogeneous.
source: As the distributions of many transcription factors in the nucleus are highly heterogeneous, the transcriptional activity of low-affinity enhancers would depend on the local microenvironments.
evidence: General knowledge about transcription factor distributions

claim: The transcriptional activity of low-affinity enhancers depends on the local microenvironments.
source: As the distributions of many transcription factors in the nucleus are highly heterogeneous, the transcriptional activity of low-affinity enhancers would depend on the local microenvironments.
evidence: Logical inference from heterogeneous TF distributions and previous observations

claim: Transcriptionally active, minimalized versions of two of the three ventral svb enhancers (E3 and 7) are Ubx-responsive.
source: Interestingly, we observed that transcriptionally active, minimalized versions of two of the three ventral svb enhancers (E3 and 7) are Ubx-responsive and preferentially appear near or overlap spatially with transcription sites of the endogenous svb gene, despite being on different chromosomes (Crocker et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2015 and Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Minimalized versions of E3 and 7 enhancers preferentially appear near or overlap spatially with transcription sites of the endogenous svb gene, despite being on different chromosomes.
source: Interestingly, we observed that transcriptionally active, minimalized versions of two of the three ventral svb enhancers (E3 and 7) are Ubx-responsive and preferentially appear near or overlap spatially with transcription sites of the endogenous svb gene, despite being on different chromosomes (Crocker et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2015 and Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Microenvironments could be shared between related enhancers to increase transcriptional output, where enhancers would synergistically form a larger local trap for transcription factors than each could alone.
source: This colocalization suggests microenvironments could be shared between related enhancers to increase transcriptional output, where enhancers would synergistically form a larger local trap for transcription factors than each could alone.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of colocalization observations

claim: Retaining multiple enhancers within a microenvironment could provide redundancy in case individual enhancers are compromised and buffer negative impacts when the system is subjected to stress.
source: Retaining multiple enhancers within a microenvironment could also provide redundancy in case individual enhancers are compromised and buffer negative impacts when the system is subjected to stress.
evidence: Hypothesis proposed based on observations

claim: svb enhancers show phenotypic robustness in maintaining sufficient trichome numbers even under temperature stress.
source: This idea is consistent with the observed phenotypic robustness of svb enhancers in maintaining sufficient trichome numbers even under temperature stress (Crocker et al., 2015; Frankel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2015 and Frankel et al., 2010

claim: The DG3 ventral enhancer contains low-affinity Ubx binding sites.
source: The ventral svb enhancers DG3, E3 and 7 (Figure 1A) contain low-affinity Ubx binding sites and have been shown to be transcribed in microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations in the first abdominal (A1) segment on the ventral surface of the embryo (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: DG3, E3 and 7 enhancers are transcribed in microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations in the first abdominal (A1) segment on the ventral surface of the embryo.
source: The ventral svb enhancers DG3, E3 and 7 (Figure 1A) contain low-affinity Ubx binding sites and have been shown to be transcribed in microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations in the first abdominal (A1) segment on the ventral surface of the embryo (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Each of the ventral svb enhancers (DG3, E3, 7) produces ventral stripes of expression along segments A1-A7 in the embryo, resembling the endogenous expression pattern of svb.
source: Each of these enhancers produces ventral stripes of expression along segments A1-A7 in the embryo, resembling the endogenous expression pattern of svb (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing expression patterns

claim: Each ventral svb enhancer contributes to different but partially overlapping portions of the total expression pattern.
source: Each enhancer contributes to different but partially overlapping portions of the total expression pattern.
evidence: Observation from expression pattern analysis

claim: The three ventral svb enhancers (DG3, E3, 7) have different Ubx ChIP enrichment profiles.
source: Furthermore, they have different Ubx ChIP enrichment profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In wild-type embryos, the DG3 reporter gene is expressed ventrally in stripes along segments A1-A7, in addition to narrow thoracic stripes in T1-T3.
source: In wild-type embryos, the DG3 reporter gene was expressed ventrally in stripes along segments A1-A7, in addition to narrow thoracic stripes in T1-T3 (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by expression data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Expression from DG3 on the ventral surface in the T2 and T3 segments is weak with wild-type Ubx expression and is primarily seen on the sides.
source: Expression from DG3 on the ventral surface in the T2 and T3 segments was weak with wild-type Ubx expression and was primarily seen on the sides.
evidence: Observation from expression pattern analysis

claim: In the absence of Ubx, DG3 reporter expression is almost completely lost on the ventral side of A1 and reduced between A2-A7.
source: In the absence of Ubx, DG3 reporter expression was almost completely lost on the ventral side of A1 and reduced between A2-A7 (Figure 1D), consistent with the responses of E3, 7 and the full svb locus (Crocker et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 1D and citation to Crocker et al., 2015

claim: The incomplete loss of DG3 expression in A2-A7 in the absence of Ubx suggests that additional factors influence the expression of ventral trichomes in those segments.
source: The incomplete loss of expression in A2-A7 suggests that additional factors influence the expression of ventral trichomes in those segments.
evidence: Inference from incomplete loss of expression

claim: Ubiquitous expression of Ubx increases DG3 expression levels in A1-A7 and generates ectopic expressions on the ventral side of the thoracic segments T2-T3 and A8.
source: Ubiquitous expression of Ubx increased the expression levels in A1-A7, in addition to generating ectopic expressions on the ventral side of the thoracic segments T2-T3 and A8 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 1E

claim: Ubx is necessary for DG3 expression in the ventral region of the abdominal segments (completely in A1 and partially in A2-7).
source: In summary, we showed that Ubx is necessary for DG3 expression in the ventral region of the abdominal segments (completely in A1 and partially in A2-7) and can induce ectopic expressions when overexpressed.
evidence: Conclusion from Ubx manipulation experiments

claim: Ubx can induce ectopic DG3 expressions when overexpressed.
source: In summary, we showed that Ubx is necessary for DG3 expression in the ventral region of the abdominal segments (completely in A1 and partially in A2-7) and can induce ectopic expressions when overexpressed.
evidence: Conclusion from Ubx overexpression experiments

claim: The Df(X)svb108 deletion allele encompasses the enhancers DG2, DG3 and Z, of which only DG3 is a ventral enhancer.
source: This svb DG3-deletion allele encompasses the enhancers DG2, DG3 and Z (Figure 2A)—of which only DG3 is a ventral enhancer.
evidence: Description of the deletion allele shown in Figure 2A

claim: Deleting a region in the svb locus containing DG3 (Df(X)svb108) leads to reduced phenotypic robustness of svb under non-optimal temperatures, with reduced numbers of trichomes produced.
source: It had been previously shown that deleting a region in the svb locus containing DG3 (Df(X)svb108) led to reduced phenotypic robustness of svb under non-optimal temperatures, with reduced numbers of trichomes produced (Frankel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frankel et al., 2010

claim: At 25°C, the Df(X)svb108 deletion allele does not show a mutant phenotype in trichome formation along the A1 and A2 segments compared to wild-type.
source: In the A1 and A2 segments at 25°C, deletion of the DG3 enhancer did not result in a clear change in ventral trichome formation in the abdominal segments compared to the wild-type (Figure 2B and C), perhaps due to the redundancy provided by overlapping expression patterns from other svb enhancers.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data in Figure 2B and C

claim: The lack of trichome phenotype at 25°C in the Df(X)svb108 deletion allele may be due to redundancy provided by overlapping expression patterns from other svb enhancers.
source: In the A1 and A2 segments at 25°C, deletion of the DG3 enhancer did not result in a clear change in ventral trichome formation in the abdominal segments compared to the wild-type (Figure 2B and C), perhaps due to the redundancy provided by overlapping expression patterns from other svb enhancers.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observation

claim: T1 trichomes are missing in larvae homozygous for the Df(X)svb108 deletion allele.
source: However, the T1 trichomes were missing in larvae homozygous for the deletion (Df(X)svb108) allele (Figure 2D and E), which we subsequently used as a homozygous marker to select for larvae homozygous for the deletion allele when crossing Df(X)svb108 flies to other lines (See 'Cuticle preparations and trichome counting' in Materials and Methods).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data in Figure 2D and E

claim: Defects in trichome formation occur in the dorsal edges of the stripe pattern in the Df(X)svb108 deletion allele, which are exclusively covered by DG3.
source: Also, we observed defects in trichome formation in the dorsal edges of the stripe pattern, which are exclusively covered by DG3 (Figure 2D and E, the black brackets at A1 and A2). This is consistent with a lack of redundancy in enhancer usage in these areas (Figure 2F, white dotted circles).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data in Figure 2D, E, and F

claim: The trichome number in regions covered by the overlapping expression of the E3, 7 and DG3 enhancers in the A1 segment does not significantly reduce at 25°C upon the deletion of DG3.
source: The trichome number in regions covered by the overlapping expression of the E3, 7 and DG3 enhancers in the A1 segment did not significantly reduce at 25°C upon the deletion of DG3 (Figure 2B,C and I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative trichome counting data in Figure 2I

claim: Larvae homozygous for the Df(X)svb108 allele developed at 32°C produce fewer trichomes compared to wild-type larvae.
source: However, larvae homozygous for the Df(X)svb108 allele developed at 32°C produced fewer trichomes compared to wild-type larvae (Figure 2G,H and I).
evidence: Supported by quantitative trichome counting data in Figure 2I

claim: Similar trichome reduction effects are observed in the A2 segment for the Df(X)svb108 allele at elevated temperature.
source: We also observed similar effects in the A2 segment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Ubx intensities around svb transcription sites with the wild-type allele do not significantly change between 25°C and 32°C in nuclei from the A1 segment.
source: In nuclei from the A1 segment, Ubx intensities around svb transcription sites with the wild-type allele did not significantly change between 25°C and 32°C (Figure 3C, bottom right panel).
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: Ubx concentrations around svb transcription sites are in general higher than the nuclear average in wild-type embryos expressing svb at 25°C.
source: Measuring Ubx intensity from random locations within nuclei of wild-type embryos expressing svb at 25°C using the same method showed that Ubx concentrations around svb transcription sites were in general higher than the nuclear average (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with our previous findings (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Transcription sites in embryos with the DG3-deletion (Df(X)svb108) allele have a local Ubx concentration that is slightly lower than wild-type at 25°C.
source: Transcription sites in embryos with the DG3-deletion (Df(X)svb108) allele had a local Ubx concentration that is slightly lower than wild-type at 25°C (Figure 3C, bottom right panel).
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: There is a clear decrease in Ubx intensity around transcription sites in DG3-deletion embryos subjected to heat-stress compared to wild-type.
source: However, there was a clear decrease in Ubx intensity compared to the wild-type when we subjected the DG3-deletion embryos to heat-stress (Figure 3B, right panel, and 3C, bottom right panel).
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3B and 3C

claim: Clear decreases in transcriptional output are detected when embryos are heat-stressed at 32°C, even with the wild-type allele.
source: Interestingly, we detected clear decreases in transcriptional output when the embryos are heat-stressed at 32°C, even with the wild-type allele.
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: The Df(X)svb108 allele at 25°C shows reduced levels of transcriptional output slightly lower than the wild-type under heat-shock.
source: The Df(X)svb108 allele at 25°C showed reduced levels of transcriptional output slightly lower than the wild-type under heat-shock.
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: At 32°C, the transcriptional output further decreases in the Df(X)svb108 mutant.
source: At 32°C, the transcriptional output further decreased in the mutant.
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 3C

claim: The various conditions tested display a weak positive correlation between svb transcriptional output and Ubx concentration (R-square = 0.4331).
source: When the various conditions were plotted by their svb transcriptional output and Ubx intensity (Figure 3C, center panel), they displayed a weak positive correlation with Ubx concentration (R-square = 0.4331).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Stress conditions reduce the transcriptional output of enhancers and the correlation to Ubx concentrations is positive but weak.
source: In sum, stress conditions reduced the transcriptional output of enhancers and the correlation to Ubx concentrations was positive but weak.
evidence: Summary of quantitative imaging data

claim: The svbBAC construct drives a dsRed reporter gene instead of another copy of svb.
source: For this purpose, we used a transgenic fly line, where a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) carrying the complete cis-regulatory region of svb (Preger-Ben Noon et al., 2018) was integrated into chromosome 2. To exclude svb mRNA from effecting the rescue, this svbBAC construct drives a dsRed reporter gene instead of another copy of svb.
evidence: Description of the experimental construct

claim: DsRed protein expression driven by the svbBAC regulatory sequence recapitulates the svb expression patterns in D. melanogaster embryos.
source: We confirmed that DsRed protein expression driven by this regulatory sequence recapitulated the svb expression patterns (Figure 4B) in D. melanogaster embryos and was responsive to Ubx—the lack of Ubx led to a decrease of expression in the A1 segment (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 4B

claim: DsRed expression driven by svbBAC is responsive to Ubx—the lack of Ubx leads to a decrease of expression in the A1 segment.
source: We confirmed that DsRed protein expression driven by this regulatory sequence recapitulated the svb expression patterns (Figure 4B) in D. melanogaster embryos and was responsive to Ubx—the lack of Ubx led to a decrease of expression in the A1 segment (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by expression data in Figure 4C

claim: In nuclei having both svb and svbBAC-dsRed transcription sites at 32°C, the distances between them are on average closer than between svb and an unrelated gene reporter construct (diBAC-gfp).
source: We observed that many active dsRed transcription sites were close to svb transcription sites in nuclei expressing both svb and dsRed in embryos from crosses between svbBAC-dsRed and wild-type (w1118) flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by distance measurements in Figure 4D

claim: The unrelated regulatory region of diachete does not show colocalization with svb.
source: This effect was not observed for the unrelated regulatory region of diachete driving the expression of gfp, which was inserted on a BAC in the same chromosomal location as svbBAC.
evidence: Negative control experiment showing specificity

claim: Both svb transcriptional output and local Ubx concentration around svb transcription sites are restored to wild-type levels when they co-localize with an active svbBAC-dsRed transcription site in the same nucleus.
source: We observed that the introduction of the svb regulatory region was able to rescue both molecular and functional defects observed from the loss of the region containing DG3. Both svb transcriptional output (Figure 4E) and local Ubx concentration around svb transcription sites (Figure 4F and G) were restored to wild-type levels, but only when they co-localized with an active svbBAC-dsRed transcription site in the same nucleus (within 360 nm from each other, see 'Analysis of distances between transcription spots' in materials and methods for the definition of colocalization).
evidence: Supported by quantitative imaging data in Figure 4E, F, and G

claim: Pairs of transcription sites under and above the 360 nm distance threshold cluster in two groups distinguishable by Ubx and svb transcription levels.
source: The pairs of transcription sites under and above this threshold clustered in two groups distinguishable also by Ubx and svb transcription levels (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis in Figure 4H

claim: Wild-type (w1118) x svbBAC-dsRed embryos and larvae are similar to wild-type in both trichome number and Ubx levels around svb transcription sites.
source: Wild-type (w1118) x svbBAC-dsRed embryos and larvae were similar to wild-type in both trichome number and Ubx levels around svb transcription sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The phenotype of ventral trichome formation on the A1 segment is partially rescued by the introduction of svbBAC to the DG3-deletion allele.
source: The phenotype, ventral trichome formation on the A1 segment (Figure 5A–C), which is reduced with the DG3-deletion allele, was partially rescued by the introduction of svbBAC (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by trichome counting data in Figure 5D

claim: The loss of the outer edge trichomes in A1 with the DG3-deletion allele is not rescued with svbBAC.
source: The loss of the outer edge trichomes in A1 (in the black brackets in Figure 5A–C, where only DG3 provides coverage Figure 2F) with the DG3-deletion allele was not rescued with svbBAC.
evidence: Supported by phenotypic data in Figure 5A-C

claim: Introducing only the DG3 enhancer as opposed to svbBAC does not rescue trichome formation under heat-stress.
source: Additionally, introducing only the DG3 enhancer as opposed to svbBAC did not rescue trichome formation under heat-stress (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by trichome counting data in Figure 5D

claim: Using multiple binding sites to ensure efficient and consistent transcriptional regulation under different environmental conditions appears to be a preferred strategy among many developmental enhancers.
source: Given the transient nature of these interactions, using multiple binding sites to ensure efficient and consistent transcriptional regulation under different environmental conditions appears to be a preferred strategy among many developmental enhancers (Frankel, 2012; Perry et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Frankel, 2012 and Perry et al., 2010

claim: Genes such as shavenbaby add another layer of redundancy through long cis-regulatory regions containing multiple enhancers whose expression patterns overlap.
source: Genes such as shavenbaby add another layer of redundancy on top of this through long cis-regulatory regions containing multiple enhancers whose expression patterns overlap.
evidence: General observation about svb regulatory architecture

claim: Redundancy in enhancers ensures proper phenotype development when systems are subjected to stress.
source: Previous works have shown that this redundancy ensures proper phenotype development when systems are subjected to stress (Crocker et al., 2015; Frankel et al., 2010; Osterwalder et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Deletion of the DG3 enhancer from svb does not lead to clear defects in ventral trichome formation unless the embryos are subjected to heat-induced stress.
source: Deletion of the DG3 enhancer from svb did not lead to clear defects in ventral trichome formation unless the embryos were subjected to heat-induced stress, as shown here and previously with the deletion of 'shadow enhancers' (Hong et al., 2008) for lateral svb expression (Frankel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by data in this study and citation to Frankel et al., 2010

claim: The DG3-deletion allele shows reduced transcriptional output even at normal temperature.
source: Nevertheless, we observed that the DG3-deletion allele showed reduced transcriptional output even at normal temperature.
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 3

claim: Wild-type embryos do not show phenotypic defects under either normal or stressed conditions.
source: Wild-type embryos did not show phenotypic defects under either normal or stressed conditions, but heat-induced stress led to slightly lower transcriptional output from the wild-type svb allele (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by phenotypic and molecular data

claim: Heat-induced stress leads to slightly lower transcriptional output from the wild-type svb allele.
source: Wild-type embryos did not show phenotypic defects under either normal or stressed conditions, but heat-induced stress led to slightly lower transcriptional output from the wild-type svb allele (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 3

claim: The mutant svb locus, starting with lower transcriptional output even under ideal conditions, drops below a threshold and the system fails under stress.
source: However, the mutant svb locus, starting with lower transcriptional output even under ideal conditions (Figure 6C), drops below a threshold and the system fails (Figure 6D).
evidence: Interpretation of the data shown in Figure 6

claim: Ubx concentration increases after a certain point are not clearly coupled to increases in svb transcriptional output.
source: We observed that Ubx concentration and svb transcriptional output in the A1 segment initially have a weak positive correlation that quickly dissipated at higher Ubx concentrations and svb outputs. While this data must be interpreted with some caution, as multiple stages of the transcription cycle are included (initiation, elongation or termination), Ubx concentration increases after a certain point were not clearly coupled to increases in svb transcriptional output.
evidence: Observation from correlation analysis in Figure 3C

claim: Additional regulatory mechanisms beyond transcription factor retention could determine the final transcriptional output of the svb locus.
source: Additional regulatory mechanisms could be at play beyond transcription factor retention that determines the final transcriptional output of the locus.
evidence: Speculation based on the weak correlation observed

claim: svb accepts inputs from many additional transcription factors, especially in the other body segments.
source: As svb also accepts inputs from many additional transcription factors (Stern and Orgogozo, 2008), especially in the other body segments, the total response of the system would also depend on many factors not observed in this study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stern and Orgogozo, 2008

claim: Transcription sites of reporter genes driven by minimal svb enhancers tend to colocalize with the endogenous svb locus when it is transcriptionally active.
source: We previously observed that transcription sites of reporter genes driven by minimal svb enhancers tended to colocalize with the endogenous svb locus when it is transcriptionally active (Tsai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2017

claim: Entire cis-regulatory regions colocalize with the svb locus, implying that they potentially share a common microenvironment.
source: This is true also for entire cis-regulatory regions, as we observed that the svb locus did the same with svbBAC, which implies that they potentially share a common microenvironment.
evidence: Inference from colocalization observations

claim: Homologous regions pair over long distances, between homologous chromosomal arms.
source: Homologous regions were shown to pair over long distances, between homologous chromosomal arms (Lim et al., 2018), translocated domains and even different chromosomes (Gemkow et al., 1998; Johnston and Desplan, 2014; Peifer and Bender, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Insulators have been described as important supporters of trans-interactions.
source: However, our constructs may not contain sites for structural elements such as insulators, which have been described as important supporters of trans-interactions (Postika et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Postika et al., 2018

claim: The observations are in line with transcription-dependent associations of interchromosomal interactions.
source: On the other hand, our observations are in line with transcription-dependent associations of interchromosomal interactions (Branco and Pombo, 2006; Joyce et al., 2016; Lomvardas et al., 2006; Maass et al., 2018; Monahan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Long range interactions may be driven, or reinforced, through shared microenvironments.
source: It is possible that such long range interactions are driven, or reinforced, through shared microenvironments.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism of long-range interactions

claim: Colocalizing with a svbBAC increases the local Ubx concentration and transcriptional output of the DG3-deletion allele.
source: High-resolution imaging showed that colocalizing with a svbBAC increases the local Ubx concentration and transcriptional output of the DG3-deletion allele (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 4

claim: Transcriptional microenvironments sequestered around large and related cis-regulatory regions in physical proximity can work in trans to increase transcriptional output of other genes, even on different chromosomes.
source: This supports a mechanism where transcriptional microenvironments sequestered around large and related cis-regulatory regions in physical proximity can work in trans to increase transcriptional output of other genes, even on different chromosomes.
evidence: Interpretation of the rescue data

claim: The introduction of a shorter reporter construct containing the DG3 enhancer alone does not rescue trichome expression perhaps because it is not able to effectively pair with the svb locus.
